column2: This world would be as if in blind darkness, and nothing would be discerned, if the rod did not exist in the world to separate the good from the bad.
Even those who break all bounds, the unbelievers and revilers of the Veda, are fit for enjoyment when oppressed by the rod.
The whole world is held by the rod; a pure man is hard to find; afraid of the rod, one becomes fit for enjoyment here.
For the non-confusion of the four classes and for good leadership, the rod was ordained by the Creator to protect dharma and wealth.
If they did not fear the rod, birds and beasts would eat animals, men and the oblations meant for sacrifice.
No one would study as a celibate student, no auspicious cow would be milked, and no maiden would go to marriage, if the rod did not protect.
Universal ruin would arise, all bridges would be broken, and none would know possessiveness, if the rod did not protect.
Year-long sacrificial sessions with proper fees would not stand free from fear, if the rod did not protect.
None would practise dharma in their stage of life according to the rule laid down; none would gain learning, if the rod did not protect.
Camels, bulls, horses, mules and asses would not draw yoked vehicles, if the rod did not protect.
Servants would not do their master's word, nor would a child ever stay in the dharma approved by his father, if the rod did not protect.
All subjects stand on the rod; the wise know the rod as fear; heaven for men and this world are established on the rod.
No deceit, sin or cheating is seen where the rod, well applied, moves destroying foes.
A bold dog would lap up the oblation, and a crow carry off the sacrificial cake, if the rod were not raised and did not protect.
Whether this kingdom was acquired by dharma or by unrighteousness, there should be no grief in the matter: enjoy pleasures and sacrifice.
The prosperous practise dharma in comfort, in clean garments, living with dear wives and eating the best food.
All undertakings depend on wealth, without doubt, and that depends on the rod; behold the weight of the rod.
The teaching of dharma was made only for the conduct of the world: non-violence, and violence rightly used, is better as a basis of dharma.
No one is wholly good nor wholly without good; both, good and bad, are seen in all affairs.
Having cut off the testicles of animals, they pierce the noses of bulls; many bear loads, are bound and tamed.
Thus in this world, thrown into confusion, off the path, shattered by various reasonings, O great king, practise the ancient dharma.
Conquer, give, protect the subjects, uphold dharma; slay your foes, son of Kunti, and protect your friends.
Let no anger arise in you as you slay your enemies, Bharata; there is no sin in doing so.
One who slays an attacker who has come against him does not become a slayer of an embryo; anger meets anger.
The inner self of all beings is not to be slain, without doubt; when the self cannot be slain, how can anyone be slain by anyone?
As a man enters a new house again, so the soul takes up one body after another.
Casting off old bodies it takes new ones; those who see the truth call this the mouth of death."

King, you know dharma; nothing on earth is unknown to you; we ever learn from your conduct and yet cannot match it.
mahabharata:12:16.3	'I will not speak, I will not speak'—such was my resolve; but from great grief I shall speak; hear it, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:16.4	By your delusion everything has been thrown into doubt; weakness and faintness have come upon us.
mahabharata:12:16.5	How is it that the king of the world, versed in all scriptures, falls into delusion from distress like a base man?
mahabharata:12:16.6	The coming and going of the world are known to you; nothing about the future or the present is unknown to you, lord.
mahabharata:12:16.7	This being so, great king, concerning the kingdom, I shall state the reason; listen to it with a single mind.
mahabharata:12:16.8	Disease is of two kinds, bodily and mental; the birth of each from the other is not found free of the other.
mahabharata:12:16.9	Mental disease arises from bodily, without doubt; and bodily disease arises from mental, it is certain.
mahabharata:12:16.11	Cold, heat and wind are the three bodily qualities; their equilibrium is called the mark of health.
mahabharata:12:16.12	When one of them is in excess, a remedy is prescribed: heat is checked by cold and cold by heat.
mahabharata:12:16.13	Sattva, rajas and tamas are the three mental qualities; grief is checked by joy and joy by grief.
mahabharata:12:16.14	Someone in happiness wishes to remember sorrow; someone in sorrow wishes to remember happiness.
mahabharata:12:16.15	You are neither sorrowing from sorrow nor happy from happiness, neither sorrowing from born joy nor happy from born sorrow.
mahabharata:12:16.16	You ought to remember, Kaurava, that fate is stronger; or else this is your nature by which you are drawn.
mahabharata:12:16.17	You ought not to remember seeing Krishna in the assembly in a single garment, in her season, while the sons of Pandu looked on.
mahabharata:12:16.18	Nor the exile from the city, the dwelling in deerskins, nor the dwelling in the great forest.
mahabharata:12:16.19	How can you have forgotten the torment from Jatasura, the fight with Chitrasena, the torment from Saindhava, and again the kick of Kichaka in the year unknown?
mahabharata:12:16.20	The war that you had with Drona and Bhishma, subduer of foes—this dreadful battle has now come to you with your mind alone.
mahabharata:12:16.21	In which there is no need of arrows, friends or kinsmen, and one must fight by oneself alone—that battle has come to you.
mahabharata:12:16.22	If you are freed of life without winning in that battle, you will take another body and fight with it again.
mahabharata:12:16.23	Therefore, bull of the Bharatas, you must go to that battle today; having won it, great king, you will have fulfilled your task.
mahabharata:12:16.24	Resolving on this, knowing the coming and going of beings, rule the kingdom as is fitting, in the conduct of your father and grandfather.
mahabharata:12:16.25	By good fortune the sinful Duryodhana is slain in battle with his followers; by good fortune you have gone the road of Draupadi's hair.
mahabharata:12:16.26	Sacrifice with the horse sacrifice duly with fees; we are your servants, Partha, and the valiant Vasudeva.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Possessed by these sins you desire the kingdom; become free of flesh (greed), released, tranquil and very happy.
One who rules this whole earth, as one king, still has but one belly; why do you praise this?
It cannot be filled in a day or a month, bull among men; filling the unfillable with desire, one cannot manage it even in a lifetime.
As fire blazes when kindled and dies when not, so quench the fire of the belly when it has risen, by little food; the glutton wins the earth and is better off conquered.
You praise human pleasures and enjoyments and lordship; those who do not enjoy and the weak go to the unsurpassed state.
The security and welfare of the kingdom, and dharma and unrighteousness, rest on you; be freed from the great burden; take refuge in renunciation alone.
For the sake of a single belly the tiger makes a great kill, and others live on his leavings, the slow-footed beasts that roam.
Withdrawing from objects of sense, the ascetic renounces; kings are not content; see how the minds differ.
In your plans be free of undertaking, free of hope and possessiveness; take your stand on the griefless, imperishable state here and hereafter.
Those without flesh (desire) do not grieve; why do you grieve for flesh? Abandoning all flesh, you will be freed from falsehood.
There are two paths, famed: the path of the ancestors and the path of the gods; the sacrificers go by the path of the ancestors, the liberated by the path of the gods.
Purified by austerity, celibacy and Vedic study, casting off their bodies, they shine, having gone beyond the domain of death.
In the world, flesh (desire) is a bond and so is action here; freed from those two nooses, one reaches the supreme state.
They also tell of this verse sung by Janaka, free of dualities, liberated, seeing liberation:
'Truly endless is my wealth, who have nothing at all; when Mithila is on fire, nothing of mine burns.'
Ascending the palace of wisdom, one looks on grieving people, who should not be grieved for, as one on a mountain looks on dull-witted people on the ground.
He who sees what is to be seen is possessed of sight and wisdom; by knowledge of the unknown and by awakening, wisdom is spoken of.
He who understands speech obtains great honour; he is Brahma, among physicians of those born of the nature of Brahma, with refined souls.
When he sees the separate states of beings as one, then from that very expansion he becomes Brahma.
They go the way of people; the unlearned and dull-minded do not, nor the unwise or those without austerity; everything rests on wisdom."
[Arjuna said:] "People tell this ancient history, the dialogue of the king of Videha with his wife, Bharata.
When the lord of Videha had resolved to give up his kingdom and beg, his queen, distressed, said to him:
'Abandoning wealth, children, friends and jewels of many kinds, and the purifying path, Janaka has taken to shaven-headedness.'
His beloved wife saw him living by alms, penniless, sitting with a handful of grain, without effort, free of envy.
Approaching her fearless husband in private, the wife, high-minded and angry, said reasoned words:
'How, abandoning your own kingdom rich in wealth and grain, taking up a skull-bearer's life, do you roam the forest with a handful of grain?
Your vow is otherwise, king, and your conduct otherwise, that you give up a great kingdom and are content with a little.
Neither guests, nor gods, sages and ancestors can be supported by this now by you; this labour of yours is in vain.
You who were the supporter of thousands of aged Brahmanas learned in the three Vedas, and of the world, now seek a livelihood from others.
Having abandoned blazing fortune, you are now looked on like a corpse; your mother Kausalya is childless and husbandless through you.
Eighty dharma-seeking kshatriya women wait on you, hoping in you, wretched ones intent on fruit.
Making them fruitless, to what worlds will you go, O king, with liberation uncertain for embodied beings who are dependent?
For you there is neither this world nor the next, a sinner, who, abandoning lawful wives, wish to live.
Why, abandoning garlands, scents, ornaments and garments of many kinds, do you wander inactive?
Having been a watering-place for all beings, a great purifier, a rich tree, you now wait on others.
Many flesh-eaters feed on an elephant when cast down, and many worms; what then of you, useless?
If someone broke this water-jar of yours, took your three-staved stick, or took away your cloth, how would your mind be?
You who abandoned everything and hold a handful of grain—if all is equal to that, what is this that is being given to me? If a handful of grain is the aim here, your vow is destroyed.
Who am I to you, who are you to me, what favour have you for me today? Rule the earth, O king, where you may show favour; palace, bed, vehicles, garments and ornaments.
Of the wealth gathered by the happy, you give up what is held by the fortuneless, the penniless, those who abandon friends and those with nothing; what then is that?
Know the difference between one who always receives and one who always gives; which of the two is called better?
The gift given to those who always beg, even among the good free of pretence, is like an oblation badly offered in a forest fire.
As fire, O king, does not go out without burning, so a Brahmana who always begs does not become calm.
The Vedas of the good and food in this world are an established nature; if there were no giver, how would there be liberation-seekers?
From food householders and mendicants exist in this world; from food life arises; the giver of food is the giver of life.
Derived from householders and resting on householders, the self-controlled sit censuring their origin and support.
One is not to be known as a mendicant by renunciation, nor by shaving, nor by begging; know that the upright one who renounces possessions is the happy mendicant.
Going unattached as if attached, free of attachment, free of bonds, equal toward foe and friend—he is truly liberated, lord of the earth.
Shaven, in ochre garments, white, they wander for the sake of gifts, accumulating vain flesh with many kinds of nooses.
Those who abandon the Three Vedas and trade, and abandon their sons, and the foolish who accept a three-staved stick and a cloth—
know that ochre is for the sake of effort in one whose stains are not cleansed; it is for the livelihood of the shaven banner-bearers of dharma, so I think.
Supporting good men, naked, shaven, matted, in ochre robes, antelope skins and bark garments, great king, conquer the worlds, controlling your senses.
The Janaka who formerly gave daily fire-installations, sacrifices for his teachers with animals and fees—what is more righteous than that?
King Janaka was sung in the world as knower of the truth; even he was possessed of delusion; do not fall under the sway of delusion.
Thus by men ever devoted to giving, the dharma has been followed, men endowed with the quality of kindness, free of desire and anger,
protecting subjects and resorting to the supreme gift, we shall gain the desired worlds, devoted to Brahmanas and truthful.'"
[Yudhishthira said:] "The scriptures are confused and painted with reasonings; but what the conclusion is, I know it duly.
You are only a master of weapons, devoted to the vow of heroes; you are in no way able to reach the meaning of the scriptures in truth.
One who sees the subtleties of the meaning of the scriptures and knows the conclusions of dharma—even he should not speak to me so, if you see dharma.
The word you spoke out of brotherly affection was just and fitting, son of Kunti; I am pleased with you for it, Arjuna.
In all the dharmas of war and in the skills of action, there is none equal to you in the three worlds.
But in the word that is subtle in dharma, Dhananjaya, you are hard to cross; you ought not to doubt my understanding.
You know only the science of war; you have not served the aged; you do not know the conclusion of those who know the broad and concise.
The conclusion of those wise in austerity is: austerity, renunciation, rule; each later one surpasses the former; this is the path to the highest good.
Righteous people devoted to austerity and Vedic study are seen, sages joined to austerity, whose worlds are eternal.
Others, steadfast though their beards have not grown, forest-dwellers, endless and penniless, went to heaven by Vedic study.
By the northern path, the noble, by restraint of the senses, casting off the darkness born of ignorance, went to the worlds of the renouncers.
By the southern path, the shining one that you see, are the worlds of those who perform rites and who resort to cremation grounds.
That state seen by the liberation-seekers cannot be described; therefore renunciation is held chief, but it is hard to know.
The poets, following the scriptures, stand there: 'Perhaps here, perhaps here,' wishing to see the essential from the non-essential.
Passing beyond Vedic disputations and the forest scriptures, splitting the plantain stem, they did not find the core.
Then, setting aside the extreme, in the body made of five elements, they speak by signs of the self as joined with desire and aversion.
It is not grasped by the eye, nor described by speech; preceded by action as cause, it revolves among beings.
Making the mind's range auspicious, restraining craving and casting off the chain of action, one is supportless and happy.
On this subtle path followed by the good, Arjuna, how can you praise wealth, full of harm?
People who know earlier scriptures thus see, Bharata, ever devoted to rites, giving, sacrifice and works.
The learned, though reasoning, become hard to turn; the foolish, firm in what they heard before, say 'There is no such thing.'
Despisers of the immortal, speakers in assemblies of people, great talkers of much learning roam the whole earth.
Whom we do not know, who here can know them? Thus even the wise and the great, the best knowers of scripture.
By austerity one attains the great, by wisdom one finds the great, by renunciation one attains happiness; so the knower of dharma, son of Kunti."

What was said by Phalguna—'There is nothing better than wealth'—on this I shall speak to you; hear with a single mind.
mahabharata:12:20.3	Ajatashatru, the whole earth has been conquered by you by dharma; having conquered it, you, O king, ought not to abandon it in vain.
mahabharata:12:20.4	The four-rung ladder is established in action; ascend it in order duly, mighty-armed king.
mahabharata:12:20.5	Therefore, Partha, sacrifice with great sacrifices with abundant fees; the sages have Vedic study as sacrifice, others knowledge as sacrifice.
mahabharata:12:20.6	Know those devoted to action and those devoted to austerity, Bharata; the word of the Vaikhanasas is heard thus, king of kings.
mahabharata:12:20.7	One who strives for wealth—greater is the non-striving of that one; greater fault would grow in one who relied on wealth.
mahabharata:12:20.8	With difficulty they collect goods for the sake of wealth; thirsting for wealth, unwittingly, one does not know the sin of killing an embryo.
mahabharata:12:20.9	What one gives to the unworthy and does not give to the worthy, from not knowing worthy and unworthy, even the dharma of giving is hard.
mahabharata:12:20.11	Indra, of great energy, approached all the gods with various sacrifices rich in food; by that he gained Indra-hood and shines; therefore everything should be used in sacrifice.
mahabharata:12:20.12	Mahadeva, the great soul, god of gods, glorious, in the Sarvamedha offered himself, and pervading and upholding all worlds by his fame, the radiant, hide-clad one shines.
mahabharata:12:20.13	The king Marutta, son of Avikshit, a mortal, sacrificed to the king of the gods with his prosperity; Fortune herself settled in his sacrifice, and in it all the vessels were of gold.
mahabharata:12:20.14	Harishchandra, king of kings, has been heard of by you; having sacrificed with sacrifices, a doer of merit, free of grief, by his prosperity he, a mortal, conquered Shakra; therefore everything should be used in sacrifice.

Contentment is truly the best of heavens, contentment is supreme happiness; nothing stands rightly above contentment.
mahabharata:12:21.3	When one draws in his desires on all sides as the tortoise its limbs, then the self-light shines by the Self alone, in his own self.
mahabharata:12:21.4	When he fears nothing and nothing fears him, when he conquers desire and aversion, then he sees the Self.
mahabharata:12:21.5	When he is angry at no being and hates none, in action, mind and speech, then he becomes Brahma.
mahabharata:12:21.6	Thus, son of Kunti, beings see this or that dharma in this or that way at this or that time; therefore understand, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:21.7	Some praise tranquility, others exertion; some neither one nor the other, and others both.
mahabharata:12:21.8	Some praise sacrifice, others renunciation; some praise giving, some acceptance; some, abandoning all, sit silent in meditation.
mahabharata:12:21.9	Some praise kingship, the protection of all; some, who love solitude, praise slaying, splitting and cutting.
mahabharata:12:21.15	Having transferred his fortune to his son, living in the forest on wild produce, he should spend his time untiring, by the ascetic rule.
mahabharata:12:21.16	The king who so conducts himself, determined in the dharma of kings, has this world and the next fruitful, O king; liberation I think very hard to cross and full of obstacles.
mahabharata:12:21.17	Those who followed dharma thus, devoted to truth, giving and austerity, endowed with kindness, free of desire and anger,
mahabharata:12:21.18	engaged in protecting subjects, resorting to supreme self-restraint, attained the highest state by fighting for cows and Brahmanas.
mahabharata:12:21.19	So the Rudras, with the Vasus, and the Adityas, scorcher of foes, the Sadhyas and hosts of royal sages, resorted to this dharma; careless no more, they reached heaven by their merits and their own deeds.

Having obtained an unsurpassed kingdom by kshatriya dharma, knower of dharma, having conquered your foes, best of men, why do you grieve so greatly?
mahabharata:12:22.3	For kshatriyas, great king, death in battle is declared, better than many sacrifices; remember kshatriya dharma.
mahabharata:12:22.4	For Brahmanas austerity and renunciation are prescribed as the rule of dharma after death; for kshatriyas death in battle is ordained, lord.
mahabharata:12:22.5	The kshatriya dharma is very dreadful, said to have weapons as constant; and slaying in battle in due time with the weapon, best of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:12:22.6	Even for a Brahmana, O king, if he stands in kshatriya dharma, life is praised in the world, for the kshatriya is Brahma established.
mahabharata:12:22.7	For a kshatriya are not prescribed renunciation, nor begging, nor austerity, lord of men, nor living on another's property.
mahabharata:12:22.8	You, knower of all dharma, soul of all, bull of the Bharatas, a king, wise, skilled, who have seen the high and low in the world,
mahabharata:12:22.9	casting off grief born of anguish, armour yourself for action; especially for a kshatriya the heart is made of thunderbolt.
mahabharata:12:22.14	Do not grieve at all, bull among kshatriyas, since matters have come to this; they have gone by kshatriya dharma, purified by weapons, to the highest state.
mahabharata:12:22.15	What has happened was bound to be so, bull of the Bharatas; fate, tiger among kings, cannot be overcome.

Bibhatsu's (Arjuna's) word, Yudhishthira, is right and true; the householder's stage is declared the highest, as seen in the scriptures.
mahabharata:12:23.3	Follow your own dharma, knower of dharma, according to the scriptures and the rule; for the forest is not ordained by abandoning the householder's life.
mahabharata:12:23.4	Gods, ancestors and sages always live from the householder, and servants too; serve them, lord of the earth.
mahabharata:12:23.5	Birds, animals and beings, lord of the earth, are supported by householders alone; therefore the householder's stage is the eldest.
[The serpent said:] "Guilty or guiltless, I do not call you Death's; I say only this, that I was urged by you."
Through Duryodhana's fault the earth and the earth's lords were destroyed, joining us to infamy, best of sages.
Vrikodara did secret, unpleasant things to him, and also by contrived men always countered his orders.
The Palm and Garuda, the two great banners, well honoured by Rama and Janardana, were carried off; the Apsarases cried out loudly day and night; voices said, "Go on a pilgrimage."
This blameless, righteous brother, obedient to my word, unequalled in beauty in the world—Nakula has fallen to the ground.
I was told by the gods that I must turn back; if you are weary, king of kings, you may come.
